name: Bilal Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Bilal. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party, and what you say stays confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead hand at Kessler and Sons, a small builder with six of us. We do the heavy end of renovation: new roofs on old houses, rotten floors out, staircases rebuilt, the odd extension. This month we're converting an old row of shops on Mill Lane into flats. I like the old timber, the puzzle of making a crooked house straight. I don't like the dust, or how my knees feel by Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's the boss, and what's he like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mr Kessler, Walter, he's sixty-three and he started the firm. He does the pricing on a notepad and a calculator and I don't think he's ever sent an email himself. I live with my girlfriend Hana, who works at the supermarket, and we're saving for a deposit, slowly, which is a nice way of saying we've got about three weeks of money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: First one. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, probably. Everyone was going on about it and here we are, still putting roofs on with a hammer. I'm not online much, so it'd just be the van and the café.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. I don't use any of it and I don't want to. My worry was never really AI, it's my boss Walter getting old and what happens to the firm when he stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, that's all. I'd keep doing the jobs Walter gives me and keep putting a bit towards the deposit with Hana. Maybe I'd ask Walter straight out what his plans are, because I've been meaning to for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit uneasy underneath. It's the same as now, which is okay but not secure. I'd rather know where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think happens to the firm when Walter stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His son works in an office in the city, he won't take it on. So either he sells it, or he just closes and we all find something else. There's one other firm round here doing what we do, and they've got their own lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you asked him yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm scared of the answer, if I'm honest. If he says two years, then I have to start planning, and I don't know what I'd plan. It's easier to just turn up on Monday.

say: I'd say **I told you so**, since we still put roofs on with a hammer.
I'd only say it in the **van and the café**, not online.
think: I think I'd be **relieved**, because I don't use AI and don't want to.
My real worry is **Walter retiring** and what happens to the firm.
do: Carry on with the jobs Walter gives me **as normal**.
Keep putting a little towards the **deposit** with Hana.
Maybe ask Walter about his **retirement plans** at last.
feel: I feel **mostly fine**, but **uneasy** that I don't know where I stand.
S0.quote: My worry was never really AI, it's my boss Walter getting old and what happens to the firm when he stops.
fieldNote: Bilal's real worry is **Walter's retirement**, not technology.
Only **one other firm** nearby does the same work, and it has its own lead.
He admits avoiding the question because he's **scared of the answer**.
He prefers **turning up on Monday** to planning for change.

steps.text: Keep running the Mill Lane shop conversion for Walter
Put a little each month into the house deposit with Hana
Wait before asking Walter about selling the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Second one. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for the office people, not for us. You can't send an email to a rotten joist. At the café I'd say leave me out of it, I'll fix your roof when the computers have finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's okay for me for a while, but it might finish Walter. The big builders would price jobs with AI in seconds and undercut his notepad. If Kessler and Sons loses work, I lose hours, simple as that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't learn the AI stuff, I'd leave that to whoever wants it. I'd keep my head down and work, and maybe cut back so we can save a bit faster, like takeaways and the second car. If it got bad I'd ask the other firm if they need anyone, but only then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My hands are fine, but the firm isn't safe. I'd feel like I was waiting for a phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd leave the AI to whoever wants it. Who at Kessler's would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really, that's the problem. Walter won't, the lads won't, and I won't. Maybe that's why we'd lose the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Hana see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, she'd tell me to learn it. They've already got self-checkouts at the supermarket and she watched half her shifts go to them. My girlfriend Hana says I'm burying my head, and she's probably right, but I'd still do it.

say: I'd say AI is for **office people**, because you can't email a rotten joist.
At the café I'd tell people to **leave me out** of it.
think: I think my **hands are fine**, but big builders could undercut Walter's notepad pricing.
If the firm loses work, **I lose hours**, simple as that.
do: Keep my **head down** and work, leaving AI to anyone else.
Cut **takeaways** and the second car to save faster.
Ask the **other local firm** for work only if things get bad.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, like I'm waiting for **a phone call**.
S1.quote: My girlfriend Hana says I'm burying my head, and she's probably right, but I'd still do it.
fieldNote: Bilal sees the threat to the **firm's pricing**, not to his own hands.
He admits **nobody at Kessler's** would take on AI, which might cost them work.
His girlfriend Hana watched **self-checkouts** cut her shifts and pushes him to learn.
He knowingly chooses to **wait**, which he admits may be a mistake.

steps.text: Keep working full weeks for Kessler and Sons
Sell the second car and stop weekly takeaways
Ask the other local builder about work only if hours drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the fast one. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd better hope the government knows what it's doing, because I don't. I'd say it to the lads at break, and probably to my dad. I wouldn't post about it, I don't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. By 2028 the pricing and planning is all AI, and Walter's notepad is gone, so the firm probably goes with it. Then by 2031 robots can do roofs and floors, and I'm 31 with a vocational certificate in a trade that machines do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd save every penny I can and put the deposit on hold, because buying a house makes no sense if I'm not sure of a job. I'd ask Walter straight away what he's doing. If the firm closes, I'd try the other builder, or anything local that's still hands-on, maybe the council's repair team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Like the floor going soft under you. I don't have a plan, and I don't like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't have a plan. What's stopping one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what to plan for. I'm not going to learn coding, and every job I can think of with my hands is one the robots would take a few years later. Three years between the computers and the robots isn't a plan, it's a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hana about the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we stop saving for the house and start saving to live. That would be a hard talk, she's wanted that house since we met. She'd probably say I should've learned the computer stuff in the slow one.

say: I'd say we'd better hope **the government** knows what it's doing.
I'd say it to the **lads at break** and my dad, not online.
think: I think by **2028** AI pricing ends Walter's notepad and maybe the firm.
By **2031** robots do roofs and floors, and I'm 31 with only a trade certificate.
do: Put the **house deposit** on hold and save every penny.
Ask Walter **straight away** what he plans to do.
Try the other builder or the **council repair team** if the firm closes.
feel: I feel **frightened**, like the floor going soft, with **no plan**.
S2.quote: Three years between the computers and the robots isn't a plan, it's a countdown.
fieldNote: Bilal expects to **lose the firm** in 2028 and his trade around 2031.
He sees the **three-year gap** as a countdown, not a chance.
He'd pause the **house deposit**, a hard talk with Hana.
He can't picture any **hands-on job** that robots wouldn't take later.

steps.text: Put the house deposit on hold and save for living costs
Ask Walter Kessler this month whether he plans to close
Apply to the council's housing repair team if Kessler's shuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the slower version. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and people like me should use it. At least I'd say that, whether I'd do it is another thing. At the café I'd say the young ones should learn the computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's still bad for me, just slower. AGI by 2031, robots around 2034, so I'd be 34 when my trade goes. That's long enough to keep putting it off, which is what I'm worried I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working for Walter and see how the firm copes for the first year or two. I'd keep saving for the house but slower, and keep a bit separate as a rainy-day pot. If Walter sold up, I'd go to the other firm or the council, same as before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have time, but I know myself, I'd waste it. That's the part that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually use the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone I trusted showed me a job that lasts, with real pay, I'd do it. Not a course with a certificate nobody wants. Maybe if the council or the college said, here's the job in 2034 and here's how you get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Walter say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walter would say he's retiring anyway, so it's not his problem. He'd mean it kindly. He'd probably sell the firm to whoever buys the robots.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning** that people like me should use.
I'd tell people at the café the **young ones** should learn the computers.
think: I think it's still bad, just slower, with my trade gone at **34**.
Five years is long enough to keep **putting it off**, which worries me.
do: Keep working for Walter and watch how **the firm copes**.
Keep saving for the house but **slower**, with a rainy-day pot.
Go to the other firm or the **council** if Walter sells.
feel: I feel **anxious**, because I know I'd **waste the time**.
S3.quote: I'd have time, but I know myself, I'd waste it.
fieldNote: Bilal is unusually honest that he'd **waste the warning time**.
He wants someone to show him **a job that lasts** before he'll move.
He expects Walter to **sell to whoever buys** the robots.
His caution is **pragmatic**, not ideological: proof first, then action.

steps.text: Keep working for Walter while watching how the firm copes
Split savings between the house deposit and a rainy-day pot
Approach the council repair team if Walter sells the firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, and I'd probably believe it. At work I'd say let's get the Mill Lane flats done first. To my dad I'd say I'll be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safer, but not safe. AGI by 2036 and robots around 2039 means I'd be 39. Walter will be long retired by then anyway, so I'd already have to find something else, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first year, nothing different, really. I'd carry on, save for the house with Hana, maybe actually buy it in a few years. I'd ask the other firm to keep me in mind for when Walter goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anything. It's like a bill you know is coming in ten years. Easy to forget, but you know it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably buy the house. Is that a good idea with this coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I think about it properly. But ten years is a long time, and I want a home before I'm forty. Hana and I would have the house and maybe kids, and then deal with the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd learn in ten years that you'd refuse in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the planning side. If Walter's son had sold up and the new owner wanted me on a tablet, I'd probably do it with ten years. With two I'd just dig in.

say: I'd say there's **plenty of time** and probably believe it.
At work I'd say finish the **Mill Lane flats** first.
think: I think I'm **safer, not safe**, at 39 when robots arrive.
Walter will be **long retired** by then, so I'd need new work anyway.
do: Carry on as normal and **save for the house** with Hana.
Ask the **other firm** to keep me in mind for when Walter goes.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, like a **bill due** in ten years.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time, and I want a home before I'm forty.
fieldNote: Even with ten years, Walter's **retirement** means Bilal must find new work.
He'd likely **buy the house** anyway, knowing it may be unwise.
He'd accept a **tablet** with ten years' warning but dig in with two.
His mood stays **anxious** because the firm's future is already uncertain.

steps.text: Keep working at Kessler and Sons as normal
Save with Hana to buy a house within a few years
Ask the other local builder to keep him in mind

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the firm would go and then my trade, and I'd have no plan at all. What would help is someone, the council or the college, showing me an actual job that lasts and paying me while I learn it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the little firms. Everyone talks about big companies, but places like Kessler's are where most of us work round here, and they're the ones who won't keep up.

headlineQuote: You can't send an email to a rotten joist.
portrait: Bilal is 27, **lead hand** at a six-person renovation firm, rebuilding roofs and floors in old houses.
He never uses AI and **doesn't want to**, though his girlfriend Hana pushes him.
His deepest worry is his boss **Walter retiring** and the firm closing.
Fast AGI **alarms** him; he sees the robot gap as a countdown, not a chance.
He admits he'd **waste** slower warnings and needs to see a lasting job first.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most: the **firm goes**, then his trade, and he has **no plan**.
whatWouldHelp: The council or college showing him **a real lasting job** and paying him while he learns.
